description: Tall tapering corn-cob shaped tower of Khmer-derived form on a stepped terrace, its whole surface encrusted with fine relief.

image.prompt:
Product photograph of one isolated object, shot from a HIGH THREE-QUARTER ANGLE: the camera is well above the object and tilted down about 30 degrees, so the top of the object is clearly visible along with its front and one side. Not a straight-on elevation.

The object: Tall tapering tower of rounded corn-cob profile on a high stepped square terrace, vertical bands of stacked receding tiers curving inward to a pointed trident finial, redented corner mouldings running the full height, a small niche with a false door on each face, steep narrow stairs up the terrace on one side Materials: Encrusted mosaic of broken porcelain shards and coloured glass over pale render, gilded trident finial, sun-bleached and lichen-spotted stonework on the terrace, dark rain runs in the vertical mouldings.

Form: build the object from a few simple, chunky, closed volumes. Prefer solid panels over lattice, mesh, grilles or perforated screens; keep any openings few, large and clearly separated. No thin spindly protrusions, no wires, no chains, no fringes, no lace, no fine filigree, no dense repeated slots or cut-outs. Keep the silhouette simple and readable from every side. Keep the object's SHAPE simple; richness must come from the surface finish, wear and materials rather than from intricate geometry. The object is still photoreal and highly detailed in its texture -- only its form is simple.

Framing: long-lens near-orthographic perspective, minimal foreshortening. The object is perfectly centred and occupies about 75% of the frame height, with clear empty margin on all four sides. The whole object is in frame; nothing is cropped.

Background: completely flat seamless neutral 50% grey (#808080). The object floats in empty space against an infinite seamless backdrop, photographed as a cut-out with nothing underneath it. There is no surface for it to rest on and nothing for it to cast a shadow onto. No floor, no ground plane, no horizon line, no cast shadow, no contact shadow, no reflection, no vignette, no gradient.

Lighting: flat even studio illumination from all sides, soft and shadowless, like a lightbox. No strong key light, no rim light, no coloured light, no specular blowout, no dramatic highlights. Colours must read as true albedo.

One object only, nothing else in frame. No people, no hands, no other props, no packaging, no text, no labels, no watermarks, no measurement annotations, no arrows, no borders, no drop shadow.

Photoreal, sharp focus edge to edge, clean and undamaged geometry, realistic materials and surface wear. Not stylised, not cartoon, not low-poly, not a 3D render preview, not a wireframe.

license.notice: Fully synthetic. No third-party scanned or scraped geometry.

review.critique: FINAL VERDICT. Overall visual fidelity 0.86 -- not a pass self-score. The shape measures 0.013 of height against the reference; the material layer, which held the first build at 0.78 with the encrustation shipped as flat cream, now carries the tile-borne surface at 0.85. 3,624/32,000 triangles, 8/24 draw calls, 5/16 materials, 8/32 unique geometries, 3 canvas textures at 4.0 MB, factory ~75-140 ms.

featureReviews.evidence: Envelope built at exactly 9.00 x 18.00 x 9.00 m, and area-weighted band comparison against the Meshy reference gives mean |delta width| 0.013 and |delta depth| 0.013 of height with every band inside 0.06 -- the closest proportional agreement of the whole batch.
featureReviews.notes: It was not close at first. Built to the plate's apparent proportions, band 2 came out 0.170 of height too wide -- the only band past the 0.12 flag anywhere in this batch. The plate is a three-quarter view from above and its foreshortening makes the platform look about a third of the prop's height; measured band by band, the reference puts the terrace top at 0.18 and shows nothing but tower across bands 2 to 5. The band table won and the terrace was rebuilt lower. The stair is the one asymmetric thing on the prop and it is cut INTO the terrace plan as a notch: hung off the outside, a flight past a 9.00 m terrace would push the bounding box off-centre and over the declared width on one side.

featureReviews.evidence: Eight receding redented tiers from 10.20 to 16.20 m, half-width 2.05 down to 0.50, each with a 0.10 m projecting ring band, closed by a lathed cap.
featureReviews.notes: The half-width follows a cosine raised to 1.5, which is what makes the taper CONVEX. A linear interpolation gives a straight cone, and a straight cone is a different building -- the corn-cob bulge is what the registry notes name as this prop's identity. Each lip starts 0.02 m above its tier's own base rather than level with it: level, the lip's underside and the tier's underside would be the same plane facing the same way, eight times over. The scalloped arch motif the plate shows on each tier is NOT authored -- thirty-two more features for detail below the resolvable band on an 18 m tower -- and the triangle headroom to add it exists and is deliberately not spent.

featureReviews.evidence: Blind arched door and raised arched pediment on each of four faces from ONE instanced unit, with eight red pilaster strips from a four-instance unit placed at radius zero.
featureReviews.notes: The pilaster system is the extreme case of the instancing lever: the unit geometry holds both strips of a single redented corner and sits at radius zero, so the four 90-degree rotations supply the four corners and the offsets are baked in -- eight parts, one geometry, one draw call. The blind door's recess is counter-intuitive and was measured rather than assumed: the plate's own recess is only slightly warmer and darker than the wall around it, so geometry rather than albedo has to carry the depth, and authoring it as a shadow would have invented a darkness the reference does not show.

featureReviews.evidence: Three notched slabs, a balustrade broken at the stair head, and a twelve-tread flight with raking cheeks -- twenty-two parts in ONE component and ONE draw call.
featureReviews.notes: Three separate z-fighting fixes here. The balustrade's side runs carry the full depth and its front and back runs stop between them, because run to full width every corner would put two outer faces in one plane facing one way. Each tread occupies only its own going rather than running back to the outer edge, so neighbours meet as opposed faces instead of twelve outer faces sharing a plane. And the slabs meet top-to-bottom, which is an opposed butt. check-coplanar reports the prop clean at 0.001 m.

name: Prang
notes: The tall slender Thai prang of the Wat Arun type: rounded corn-cob profile, encrusted porcelain surface, trident finial. It is deliberately a separate asset from a Khmer stone sanctuary even though both descend from the same Khmer tower form, because they read as completely different objects -- this one is tall, slim, pale and encrusted, while the Khmer original is squat, dark sandstone and ruined. Declared at 18 m, well above the building-part category's 8 m prior, which is correct for a riverside prang. No destruction groups: it is static landmark geometry.
